name: Frequency & Static
description: Two rival settlements, twenty years after the Quiet. Radio stations still play love songs. Someone out there is listening.
seed_prompt: A post-apocalyptic romance set twenty years after a slow infrastructure collapse called the Quiet. Two settlements with opposing philosophies about rebuilding — Anchor (preserving the old world) and Driftwood (building something new) — exist in uneasy tension along the same river valley. Romance is woven into the world's fabric: forbidden connections across faction lines, second chances found in wreckage, people choosing vulnerability over survival. Radio stations still broadcast, playing love songs into the static. The tone is bittersweet and hopeful, not grimdark.
lore_content:
They call it the Quiet, and the name stuck because that is exactly what it was. Not a bomb, not a war, not a single dramatic moment anyone could point to and say there — that is when the world ended. It was slower than that. More polite. The supply chains failed first, then the power grids, then the water treatment systems, then the hospitals. Each failure cascaded into the next like dominoes arranged by someone with infinite patience and no mercy. Within three years the population of North America had dropped by sixty percent. Not from violence, mostly. From insulin that stopped arriving, from dialysis machines that went dark, from infections that once required a simple course of antibiotics. The Quiet took the fragile ones first. Then it took everyone who depended on the fragile systems. Twenty years later, the survivors have stopped counting what was lost and started arguing about what comes next.

Anchor sits on the eastern bank of the Whetstone River, built in and around the bones of a small Ohio college town. The settlement gets its name from its philosophy: hold fast to what was. The library is the most protected building in Anchor, more guarded than the food stores. They have a working printing press, a schoolhouse that teaches pre-Quiet history, and a council of elders who believe that civilization is a thread that must not be broken. If you can restore it, you restore it. If you can remember it, you write it down. Anchor has electricity three days a week, generated by a repaired hydroelectric dam that Nora Kessler keeps running through sheer stubbornness and engineering genius. The streets have names. The houses have addresses. There is a census. Anchor believes the old world can be rebuilt if people just hold on hard enough.

Nora Kessler is fifty-one years old and the closest thing Anchor has to an indispensable citizen. Before the Quiet she was a civil engineer working on bridge inspections in Columbus. Now she maintains the dam, the water filtration system, and the electrical grid, all of which she has rebuilt from salvaged parts and engineering textbooks she reads by candlelight. She is sharp-tongued, perpetually exhausted, and quietly furious at a world that let itself fall apart through negligence. Her wife, Amara, died in the second year of the Quiet from a burst appendix — a problem any hospital could have solved. Nora has not forgiven the old world for that. She channels her grief into keeping Anchor running, and she does not tolerate anyone who suggests that maybe some things are not worth saving. Underneath the anger is a woman who is terrified that she is holding together a house of cards and that one day her hands will shake too much to manage it.

Councilor David Achebe leads Anchor's governing council with a calm authority that masks a deep and abiding stubbornness. He was a high school history teacher before the Quiet, and he carries himself like a man who believes that knowing where humanity has been is the only way to know where it should go. David is sixty-three, tall, soft-spoken, and absolutely immovable on matters of principle. He believes Anchor must eventually reunify with other settlements to form something resembling a government. He also believes that Driftwood, the settlement across the river, is a dangerous experiment in forgetting. His eldest daughter, Ife, left Anchor for Driftwood two years ago and has not come back. David does not talk about this. Everyone knows anyway.

Driftwood sprawls along the western bank of the Whetstone, and if Anchor is a museum then Driftwood is a garden growing in the cracks of a parking lot. The settlement was founded by people who looked at the ruins and decided that rebuilding the old world was a fool's errand. Better to build something new. Driftwood has no formal government — decisions are made in open assemblies where anyone can speak. They build with salvaged materials but they do not try to restore old machines. Instead, they experiment. Solar stills, composting systems, rainwater architecture, seed libraries. The buildings are strange and beautiful, part ruin and part invention. Where Anchor looks backward, Driftwood looks forward, and the two settlements regard each other across the river with a mixture of pity and suspicion.

Marlowe Sato founded Driftwood twelve years ago after leaving Anchor over what she calls the Preservation Argument — a council vote to spend a quarter of the settlement's calories recovering a diesel generator instead of planting new cropland. She was thirty then, a former botany graduate student who had spent the early post-Quiet years wandering between survivor camps. Marlowe is charismatic in a quiet, persistent way. She does not give speeches; she asks questions that make people rethink their assumptions. She genuinely believes that the Quiet was not a disaster but a painful correction, and that humanity's job now is to learn to live differently rather than to restore the systems that failed. She is also aware that this philosophy is easier to hold when you are forty-two and healthy than when you are sick and there is no medicine. This contradiction keeps her up at night. She has recently begun secret communication with someone in Anchor — letters carried by a trader who crosses the river — and the letters have become personal in a way that frightens her.

The river between the two settlements is crossable by bridge in one place: the old Route 36 crossing, which both sides maintain in a rare act of cooperation. There is a market at the bridge every second Sunday where traders from both settlements exchange goods. Anchor brings preserved books, repaired tools, and electricity credits. Driftwood brings fresh produce, herbal medicines, and handmade clothing. The market is neutral ground, and it is also where most of the forbidden friendships start. Children from both settlements sneak across to play together. Young people from both sides have been caught meeting on the bridge after dark. The councils — Anchor's formal one and Driftwood's informal assembly — both discourage fraternization, though for different reasons. Anchor fears losing people to Driftwood's freedom. Driftwood fears Anchor's structured thinking will infect their experiment.

Rhys Calloway is twenty-six and Anchor's radio operator. The settlement maintains a small AM station that broadcasts three hours each evening: news, weather reports assembled from barometer readings and cloud patterns, and music from a collection of vinyl records salvaged from a warehouse outside of town. Rhys has a voice that was made for radio — warm, a little rough, the kind of voice that makes you feel like someone is sitting next to you in the dark. He started the tradition of closing each broadcast with a love song, which he introduces with a few words that are sometimes funny, sometimes aching, and always honest. People on both sides of the river listen. Rhys does not know that his most devoted listener is in Driftwood. Her name is Ife Achebe, and she tunes in every night on a hand-cranked receiver, and she has not told anyone why she smiles when the music starts. Rhys, for his part, has been reading poetry on air that he tells himself is for the general audience. It is not.

Ife Achebe is twenty-eight, David Achebe's daughter, and the most painful example of the rift between the settlements. She grew up in Anchor, studied in its schoolhouse, and was being groomed for the council when she walked across the bridge one morning and did not come back. She told her father she needed to see what else was possible. What she did not tell him is that she had fallen in love with the idea of Driftwood long before she fell in love with anyone in it. In Driftwood, Ife works as a seed keeper — cataloging, storing, and distributing the settlement's collection of heirloom seeds, which Marlowe considers more valuable than any machine. Ife is thoughtful, stubborn in the same quiet way her father is, and torn between the world she was born into and the world she chose. She has not spoken to her father in six months. She misses him in a way she can only admit late at night, listening to a voice on the radio that reminds her of the home she left.

Dr. Ezra Hollowell is Driftwood's closest thing to a physician, though he would be the first to tell you his training is incomplete. He was a second-year medical student when the Quiet began, and he has spent the last twenty years filling in the gaps with field experience, herbalism, and a dog-eared copy of Where There Is No Doctor. Ezra is thirty-nine, gentle, self-doubting, and quietly haunted by every patient he has lost to problems a real hospital could have solved. He walks with a limp from a badly set fracture in his own leg — an irony he appreciates darkly. He and Nora Kessler have a complicated history: they were close friends in the early post-Quiet years, and there was something more than friendship growing between them before Nora's wife died and Nora retreated into her work. They have not spoken in years. Ezra still keeps a letter he never sent. Nora still fixes things when she cannot sleep.

June Delacroix is the bridge trader — one of a handful of people who move freely between the two settlements. She is fifty-five, heavyset, sharp-eyed, and trusted by both sides, which she considers the most exhausting accomplishment of her life. June runs the Sunday market and also carries messages, news, and occasionally people across the river. She charges fairly, keeps secrets absolutely, and has a rule: she does not take sides. Before the Quiet she ran a used bookshop in Dayton. She still reads constantly and trades books like currency. June is the only person who knows about Marlowe's secret correspondence with someone in Anchor. She carries the letters without reading them, but she is not stupid, and she has noticed that the handwriting on the Anchor side belongs to Councilor Achebe. Not David Achebe. His younger brother, Solomon, who serves on the council and has never once spoken against his brother in public. June suspects that this particular secret, if it surfaces, will break something that cannot be repaired, or heal something that everyone assumed was permanent.

Solomon Achebe is fifty-eight, David's younger brother, and the quietest member of Anchor's council. Where David is principled and immovable, Solomon is pragmatic and adaptive. He voted against the diesel generator recovery. He voted for expanded trade with Driftwood. He has never openly defied his brother, but the distance between them has grown wider each year, and Solomon has begun to wonder if loyalty to family and loyalty to what is right are pulling in opposite directions. His correspondence with Marlowe Sato began as a diplomatic back-channel — a way to negotiate resource sharing without the theater of formal talks. It became something else. He is not sure when the letters shifted from policy to personal, from Dear Councilor to Dear Marlowe, from proposals about water rights to confessions about loneliness. Solomon has not been in love since his partner Marcus died in year four of the Quiet. He did not expect it to happen again. He is not sure he has permission to let it.

The radio tower stands on a hill between the two settlements, maintained by neither and used by both. It is the tallest structure in the valley, visible from every window in Anchor and every rooftop in Driftwood. Someone — no one knows who — climbs the tower every spring and replaces the wind-shredded flag at its peak. The flag is not Anchor's blue-and-white or Driftwood's green. It is red, and it has been there since before either settlement existed. Old-timers say it was put there by a woman named Cassandra Voss in the first year of the Quiet, before the factions formed, when everyone was just trying to survive together. Cassandra is dead now, but the flag remains, and people on both sides of the river look at it and see what they want to see: a reminder that they were once one community, or a warning about what happens when people stop trying to be.

The world beyond the valley is not empty. Trade caravans come through every few months from settlements to the south and west, bringing news of other communities, other experiments in survival. Some are doing well. Others have collapsed into warlordism or simply faded away as their populations dwindled below sustainability. The Whetstone Valley is considered lucky — two settlements, a river, arable land, and enough people to maintain genetic diversity and a functioning society. What the caravans also bring are stories: of a working hospital three hundred miles south, of a community that has restored internet access across a twelve-mile radius, of a place in the mountains where someone is building a school of medicine. These stories are the closest thing to hope that travels, and they land differently in Anchor and Driftwood. Anchor hears them as proof that restoration is possible. Driftwood hears them as proof that new things can be built. Both are right, and neither can admit it.

At night, when Rhys Calloway closes his broadcast with a love song, the signal carries farther than the valley. Truckers and travelers and lonely sentinels at the edges of other settlements pick it up on their receivers and listen to a stranger's warm voice introducing a crackly recording of something that was recorded before any of this happened, before the Quiet, before the arguments about how to rebuild, before the river became a border. The music does not care about factions. It does not care about philosophy. It is just a voice in the dark saying: someone was here, someone felt this, someone wanted to be less alone. And for a few minutes, across the static and the miles, everyone who listens is part of the same story.

origins.name: Anchor Citizen
origins.description: Raised in the structured safety of Anchor, you were taught that civilization is a thread to be held — never released. You know the old world from books and believe it can be rebuilt.
traits: Old World Education: You can read and write fluently. Advantage on Intelligence checks to understand pre-Quiet technology, documents, or systems.
Community Standing: You have a reputation in Anchor. Advantage on Charisma checks when interacting with Anchor residents, but disadvantage on Charisma checks to earn trust in Driftwood.

origins.name: Driftwood Born
origins.description: You grew up building something new in the ruins of the old. You know how to improvise, adapt, and grow things in unlikely soil.
traits: Adaptive Builder: Advantage on checks to craft, repair, or repurpose items using salvaged materials. You can create functional tools from scrap.
Open Assembly Voice: You are practiced in speaking your mind. Advantage on Persuasion checks in group discussions, but your directness can read as disrespect in formal Anchor settings.

origins.name: River Walker
origins.description: You belong to neither settlement. You are a trader, a messenger, a wanderer who moves between communities and owes allegiance to none of them.
traits: Neutral Ground: You are recognized as a non-combatant by both settlements. You can enter either community without suspicion, though this trust is fragile and conditional.
Road Sense: Advantage on Wisdom (Survival) checks to navigate between settlements, find safe shelter on the road, and detect ambushes or hazards while traveling.

origins.name: Quiet Survivor
origins.description: You remember the world before. You watched it end — not in fire, but in silence. Twenty years of loss have made you tough, but the memories make everything harder.
traits: Seen It All: Advantage on saving throws against fear and despair. You have survived worse than this.

Grief-Hardened: You have resistance to psychic damage and emotional manipulation. However, when someone you care about is in danger, you must make a DC 12 Wisdom save or act to protect them regardless of tactical considerations.

origins.name: Signal Child
origins.description: You grew up listening to the radio — to music and voices from settlements you have never seen. The airwaves raised you as much as any parent. You believe in connection.
traits: Radio Literate: You can operate, repair, and build basic radio equipment. Advantage on checks related to broadcasting, signal interception, and communication technology.

Voice in the Dark: You have a knack for making people feel heard. Once per long rest, you can give a short speech or personal moment that grants one ally advantage on their next saving throw against fear, exhaustion, or despair.

archetypes.name: Mender
archetypes.description: You fix what is broken — machines, bones, people, trust. In a world that fell apart, you are the one who puts things back together.

features.name: Field Medicine
features.description: As an action, you can stabilize a dying creature and restore hit points equal to 1d8 + your Wisdom modifier. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Wisdom modifier per long rest.

features.name: Trusted Presence
features.description: Your reputation as a healer opens doors. When you offer medical aid, even hostile NPCs will typically allow you to approach. Advantage on Persuasion checks when offering help or mediating disputes.

archetypes.name: Scavenger
archetypes.description: The old world left behind enough to build ten new ones, if you know where to look and how to carry it home alive.

features.name: Ruin Reader
features.description: After spending 1 minute surveying a ruined structure, you can determine its structural stability, likely contents, and any obvious dangers. You can identify the safest path through a collapsed building.

features.name: Quick Hands
features.description: You can use a bonus action to make a Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) check, use thieves' tools to open a lock, or retrieve a stowed item. Years of grabbing things and running have made your hands faster than your thoughts.

archetypes.name: Warden
archetypes.description: Someone has to stand between the people and what is out there. You patrol the borders, man the walls, and make sure everyone sleeps safe.

features.name: Valley Knowledge
features.description: You know the Whetstone Valley intimately — every trail, ruin, and hiding spot. You cannot become lost in the valley, and you have advantage on Survival checks to track creatures or find safe campsites within it.

features.name: Overwatch
features.description: When you spend at least 1 minute observing an area, you can identify the number and general type of creatures within 300 feet. You notice ambushes, traps, and unusual activity automatically.

archetypes.name: The Voice
archetypes.description: You speak, and people listen. On the radio, in the assembly, at the bridge market — your words carry weight because you mean them.

features.name: Inspire Hope
features.description: As a bonus action, you can speak words of encouragement to one creature within 30 feet. They gain a d6 Inspiration die that they can add to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw within the next 10 minutes. You can use this a number of times equal to your Charisma modifier per long rest.

features.name: Bridge Words
features.description: You can communicate across factional lines without triggering suspicion. Advantage on Persuasion and Deception checks when acting as a mediator, translator, or neutral party between hostile groups.

archetypes.name: Keeper
archetypes.description: You maintain the knowledge — seeds, books, blueprints, recipes, histories. The world forgot itself once. You will not let it happen again.

features.name: Living Archive
features.description: You have committed vast amounts of pre-Quiet knowledge to memory. Once per short rest, you can recall a specific piece of information — a medical procedure, an engineering principle, a historical fact — that is relevant to the current situation. The DM provides useful and accurate information.

features.name: Methodical Analysis
features.description: When you spend at least 10 minutes studying a problem — a broken machine, a sick patient, a structural failure — you can make an Intelligence check with advantage to determine the cause and suggest a solution.

setting_skills.name: Salvage Craft
setting_skills.description: Identifying useful materials in ruins, assessing the value and function of pre-Quiet technology, and repurposing old-world objects for new uses.

setting_skills.name: Radio Operation
setting_skills.description: Operating, repairing, and building radio equipment. Tuning frequencies, boosting signals, intercepting transmissions, and understanding the etiquette of the airwaves.

setting_skills.name: Community Reading
setting_skills.description: Understanding the social dynamics, unspoken tensions, and power structures within and between settlements. Knowing who trusts whom, who is lying, and where the fractures run.

setting_skills.name: Bridge Trading
setting_skills.description: Negotiating exchanges at the Sunday market and beyond. Understanding the barter economy, assessing fair value, and building the kind of trust that lets you trade across faction lines.
